strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in camera-controlled video generation: preserving scene content when revisiting previously observed regions. Keeping per-frame geometry separate and reconciling rendered anchors during generation is a well-motivated alternative to fusing inconsistent reconstructions.

The framework coherently combines coverage-driven retrieval, cross-anchor attention, pose-conditioned fusion, and explicit camera control. Its integration with both CogVideoX and Wan2.2 supports applicability beyond one backbone.

Multi-anchor conditioning produces meaningful reconstruction gains. On CogVideoX, increasing K from 1 to 4 improves PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727. Table 1 also reports competitive reconstruction fidelity and stronger aggregate video-quality scores than the evaluated baselines.

The qualitative examples illustrate complementary anchor coverage and plausible preservation of scene content across generated segments. The appendix provides useful training details and transparently identifies reimplemented baselines.
weaknesses: The central long-horizon claim is insufficiently evaluated. The quantitative protocol reconstructs 49 target frames using 21 interleaved context frames from the same 70-frame sequence; it does not test accumulated errors when repeatedly updating memory with generated content. Long-horizon evidence consists of selected examples up to 241 frames, without quantitative revisit measurements, comparative rollouts, or degradation curves. These examples establish feasibility more convincingly than sustained world consistency.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the principal contributions. Table 2 changes both global versus local memory and single versus multiple anchors, confounding geometry representation with conditioning capacity and access to separate observations. Pose-guided fusion and shared attention receive only qualitative examples, while coverage-driven retrieval is not compared quantitatively against random, pose-nearest, or overlap-based selection at a fixed anchor budget.

Important geometric and implementation details remain unspecified: how newly reconstructed segments are aligned to the existing world coordinate system, how coverage and occlusion are computed, the FoV filtering threshold, and how pose-derived fusion weights are normalized and aligned with temporally compressed latents. These details directly affect reproducibility and robustness to the pose errors motivating the method. The controller schedule also differs between the main text and appendix: 90% versus 80% of denoising steps.

The comparisons support competitive performance but warrant more restrained claims. SEVA achieves higher PSNR than both full AnchorWeave variants, with nearly identical SSIM. The closest memory baselines are reimplementations whose fidelity to the original methods is not validated, and uncertainty estimates are absent. The manuscript should also explicitly identify held-out evaluation splits and clarify the 49-frame evaluation procedure for the Wan2.2 model trained on 81-frame clips.

Scalability is asserted without inference-time or memory measurements. Per-frame point-cloud storage grows with history, retrieval requires evaluating candidates, and joint attention operates over concatenated anchor tokens. Runtime and storage scaling with history length and anchor count are needed to substantiate the claimed scalable long-horizon use. Overall, the promising design and reconstruction results leave the decision close, but the missing validation of the central claim favors rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: preserving scene structure when camera-controlled generation revisits previously observed regions. Keeping per-frame geometry separate and reconciling rendered anchors during generation is a sensible alternative to committing to imperfect global fusion.

The proposed framework is coherent and clearly illustrated. Coverage-based retrieval, joint cross-anchor attention, and pose-conditioned fusion provide complementary mechanisms for using spatial memory.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence that additional local anchors improve reconstruction. On CogVideoX, increasing K from 1 to 4 raises PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727. Results on two backbones and the qualitative comparisons support the approach's practical promise.

The authors make useful efforts toward comparison and reproducibility: single-anchor baselines receive retrieved geometric conditioning, a K=1 variant is included, and the appendix describes training settings and the reimplementation of unavailable baselines.
weaknesses: The central long-horizon claim is insufficiently evaluated. Section 4.1 generates 49 target frames with 21 real context frames interleaved within the same 70-frame sequence. This is a useful partial-revisit benchmark, but it does not measure repeated memory updates from generated observations or accumulating drift. Long-horizon evidence consists of selected examples extending to 241 frames, without quantitative revisit measurements or matched baseline rollouts.

The ablations do not adequately establish the contributions of the proposed components. Table 2 changes both memory representation and conditioning multiplicity, comparing one global anchor against multiple local anchors. Figure 5 provides only qualitative examples for joint attention and pose-guided fusion. There is no quantitative comparison of coverage-driven retrieval against random, pose-nearest, or overlap-based retrieval at a fixed anchor budget, despite retrieval being a central contribution.

Avoiding fusion does not eliminate errors in depth or the shared coordinate system. Section 3.2 still transforms estimated local memories into common world coordinates, but the manuscript does not sufficiently explain how incremental reconstructions remain aligned across generated segments. Controlled tests of pose/depth error and conflicting memories are needed to substantiate the claim that the controller reliably reconciles these errors.

The strongest numerical comparisons support a narrower conclusion than the text suggests. SEVA achieves higher PSNR than either full AnchorWeave variant, while SSIM differences are small: 0.6711 versus 0.6727/0.6739. AnchorWeave improves several temporal-quality measures, but no uncertainty estimates are reported. The reimplemented memory baselines are useful, yet their fidelity to the original methods is not validated, limiting conclusions about superiority over those approaches.

Important implementation and scalability details remain unspecified: train/test scene separation, rendering and visibility rules, FoV filtering thresholds, pose-weight normalization, and inference resolution. The controller is described as active for 90% of denoising steps in Section 4.1 but 80% in Appendix A.1. No inference-time or memory-growth measurements support the scalability claim, despite retaining per-frame point clouds and jointly attending over multiple anchor sequences.

strengths: Under Algorithms/General, the paper presents a coherent contribution to memory-conditioned video generation: retaining separate local geometric memories avoids baking cross-view fusion artifacts into a single conditioning video, while joint attention and pose-guided fusion reconcile complementary anchors during generation. This is a useful design distinction from the cited global-memory approaches.

The multi-anchor benefit is supported quantitatively on the 500-video partial-revisit evaluation. With CogVideoX, increasing K from 1 to 4 improves PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727, with intermediate improvements at K=2. Similar gains with Wan2.2 support applicability across backbones.

The method offers a favorable consistency–temporal-quality tradeoff. Its reconstruction scores are competitive with SEVA, while motion smoothness and temporal flickering scores improve. Figure 4 also illustrates better preservation of scene details in several examples.

The manuscript clearly explains the overall architecture and supplies retrieval pseudocode, training settings, and baseline reimplementation details. Free-form trajectory examples and 241-frame rollouts provide encouraging qualitative evidence beyond the principal benchmark. Collectively, these merits support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative protocol does not directly establish long-horizon world consistency. It generates 49 target frames using 21 interleaved observations from the same 70-frame video, providing nearby reference views throughout the trajectory. This is a useful reconstruction setting, but does not measure error accumulation when repeatedly updating memory from generated content. The long-horizon evidence consists of selected qualitative rollouts, without quantitative revisit comparisons or degradation curves across generation cycles.

The component evidence is incomplete. Coverage-driven retrieval is not compared against random, pose-nearest, or overlap-based retrieval at a matched anchor budget. Pose-guided fusion and joint attention receive only qualitative ablations. Table 2 changes both memory representation and the number of conditioning anchors, so its large improvement cannot be attributed solely to avoiding global fusion. Matched conditioning and quantitative component ablations would strengthen the causal argument.

The breadth of superiority claims exceeds the results. SEVA has higher PSNR than both full AnchorWeave variants, and ViewCrafter has higher imaging quality. Several aggregate quality gains are modest and lack uncertainty estimates. The strongest supported conclusion is competitive reconstruction with improved temporal metrics, rather than uniformly superior reconstruction and perceptual quality.

Comparisons with the closest memory-based methods depend on author reimplementations. Matching data and training steps is helpful, but Context-as-Memory uses rank-16 LoRA whereas AnchorWeave trains additional controller modules; comparable capacity and adequate tuning are not established. These comparisons should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Important reproducibility and scalability details remain unclear: scene-disjoint training/evaluation splits, coverage rasterization and FoV thresholds, and incremental alignment of newly estimated geometry into the existing world coordinate system. Local memories avoid fusion artifacts but still depend on pose and depth accuracy. No runtime or memory-growth measurements substantiate scalability, particularly with joint attention over K times as many anchor tokens. The main text and appendix also disagree on using the controller for 90% versus 80% of denoising steps.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: preserving scene identity during camera-controlled exploration and revisits. Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, its central idea—retaining separate local geometric memories and learning to reconcile their rendered anchors—is well motivated and meaningfully distinguishes it from globally fused memory approaches.

The architecture coherently combines complementary-coverage retrieval, cross-anchor attention, and pose-conditioned fusion. The pipeline figures and qualitative comparisons help explain how separate anchors preserve useful evidence despite inconsistent geometry.

The quantitative evaluation covers 500 videos and two diffusion backbones. Increasing the anchor budget from K=1 to K=4 improves CogVideoX PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727, with similar improvements for Wan2.2. This provides credible evidence that multiple local anchors improve historical-context reconstruction.

The appendix provides meaningful long-horizon evidence: an explore-and-revisit experiment from 20 initial images extends to 2,400 frames and shows substantially better revisit PSNR than the reimplemented SPMem baseline. This supplements the shorter partial-revisit benchmark and qualitative demonstrations.

The paper reports computational costs, history-length scaling, training settings, and baseline reimplementation details. Its discussion of accumulated synthesis errors, pose drift, reflective surfaces, and dynamic-object masking appropriately acknowledges the method's scope. Overall, the demonstrated benefits support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The ablations do not adequately isolate several central contributions. Table 2 changes both the memory representation and the number of conditioning anchors when comparing global and local memory. Pose-guided fusion and joint attention are supported only by selected qualitative examples, while coverage-driven retrieval lacks a quantitative comparison with random, pose-nearest, or overlap-based selection at the same anchor budget. Consequently, the evidence establishes the usefulness of the complete system more clearly than the necessity of its proposed components.

The main 500-video benchmark interleaves 21 observed context frames with 49 target frames sampled from the same 70-frame sequence. This is a useful historical-view reconstruction test, but does not itself test accumulated errors in autoregressive exploration. The appendix partially addresses this through repeated returns to the initial pose, although it compares only against reimplemented SPMem and reports no variability across the 20 scenes. Broader claims about persistent world consistency remain less established than reconstruction of previously observed views.

The comparison against global memory depends strongly on how that baseline is constructed. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify global-cloud alignment, confidence filtering, fusion, or pruning. The rendering diagnostic and SPMem's eventual memory failure therefore demonstrate limitations of the implemented fusion pipeline, rather than establishing that global representations generally fail. A controlled comparison using a filtered or bounded global memory would strengthen the central argument.

Several details needed for reproduction are ambiguous. Algorithm 1 initializes retrieval with the latest memory, whereas the baseline description says K=1 selects the maximum-coverage memory and other passages describe fixing the first frame. These alternatives affect both the claimed matched K=1 comparison and the retrieval ablation. The paper also leaves the coverage/occlusion calculation, FoV threshold, pose-weight normalization, and incremental alignment into shared world coordinates insufficiently specified. Training/test scene separation should be stated explicitly.

Some claims exceed the reported results. SEVA has higher PSNR than either full AnchorWeave backbone in Table 1, while AnchorWeave's SSIM advantage is small and lacks uncertainty estimates; its clearer advantage is in the reported aggregate and temporal quality metrics. Thus, statements that it outperforms all baselines across reconstruction and quality should be qualified. Minor reporting inconsistencies also need correction: controller use during 90% versus 80% of denoising steps, SSIM scaling in Table 2, and the duplicated TrajCrafter row in Table 5.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in camera-controlled video generation: preserving previously observed scene content despite imperfect geometry. Retaining separate local memories and learning to reconcile their rendered anchors is a coherent contribution under Algorithms/General.

The quantitative results support the usefulness of multi-anchor conditioning. On CogVideoX, increasing K from 1 to 4 improves PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727. Similar improvements on Wan2.2 strengthen the evidence that the approach transfers across backbones.

Evaluation includes 500 videos, several relevant baselines, qualitative free-form camera trajectories, and an explicit performance–cost comparison. Reimplementing the unavailable memory baselines with the same backbone and training data is a useful effort toward comparability.

Appendix H.2 provides substantive long-horizon evidence beyond the short partial-revisit benchmark: a 20-image explore-and-revisit experiment extending to 2,400 frames shows substantially better retention than the SPMem reimplementation. The discussion candidly identifies pose drift, feedback of synthesis errors, reflections, and dynamic-content limitations.
weaknesses: The ablations do not adequately isolate several central contributions. Table 2 changes both memory representation and the number of conditioning anchors. Pose-guided fusion and shared attention are supported only by individual qualitative examples in Figure 5, and coverage-driven retrieval is not quantitatively compared with random, nearest-pose, or overlap-based retrieval at a fixed budget. Consequently, the benefits of the complete system are better established than the necessity of its particular components.

The principal benchmark uses 21 context frames interspersed with 49 target frames from the same 70-frame sequence. This is useful for measuring reconstruction from observed context, but does not directly test causal memory accumulation during exploration. The appendix stress test partially addresses this gap, although its metric measures returns to the initial view, with only one comparator and no reported uncertainty; it does not establish consistency throughout newly explored regions.

The case against global memory depends on the specific fusion implementation. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify its filtering, confidence handling, or geometric alignment, nor compare against a more robustly fused or pruned global representation. The rendering diagnostic demonstrates degradation for the chosen construction, but does not establish that global representations generally suffer the claimed disadvantage. Likewise, SPMem's eventual rendering failure is partly an implementation-dependent scalability result.

Important reproduction details remain ambiguous: the exact train/test split and scene disjointness, coverage and FoV-overlap calculations, pose-weight normalization, and incremental alignment of new memories to the persistent coordinate system. There are also conflicting descriptions of the denoising control schedule (90% in Section 4.1 versus 80% in Appendix A.1) and initial-anchor selection (first frame, latest memory, or maximum-coverage retrieval in different passages). These ambiguities affect faithful implementation and interpretation of K=1 comparisons.

Some conclusions overstate the results. SEVA has higher PSNR than either full AnchorWeave variant, while the SSIM advantage is small and lacks uncertainty estimates. The evidence supports competitive reconstruction with better reported temporal metrics, rather than uniformly superior reconstruction. Despite these reservations, the coherent design, reproducible trend across two backbones, and additional long-horizon evidence support a slight preference for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in camera-controlled video generation: preserving scene identity across revisits despite imperfect geometry. Under Algorithms/General, its central contribution is a coherent and useful combination of separate local geometric memories, coverage-driven retrieval, and learned multi-anchor reconciliation.

The quantitative evidence supports the value of multiple anchors. On CogVideoX, increasing K from 1 to 4 improves PSNR from 19.01 to 20.96 and SSIM from 0.6145 to 0.6727. Results on two backbones strengthen the case that the approach is broadly applicable. Compared with SEVA, AnchorWeave offers comparable reconstruction fidelity and better reported temporal-quality metrics.

The supplementary material meaningfully strengthens the long-horizon evidence. The 20-image explore-and-revisit experiment extends to 2400 frames and shows substantially better consistency than the reimplemented SPMem baseline. Camera-control evaluation, qualitative free-form trajectories, and retrieval/rendering scaling measurements provide useful complementary evidence.

The presentation clearly motivates the design and illustrates complementary anchor coverage. Computational costs are reported transparently, including the increase from 221 to 275 seconds and 34 to 39 GB for multi-anchor generation. The discussion of pose drift, accumulated synthesis errors, reflections, and static-memory limitations appropriately bounds the claims.
weaknesses: The ablations do not adequately isolate several central contributions. Pose-guided fusion and joint attention are supported only by selected qualitative examples, and coverage-driven retrieval is not quantitatively compared with random, nearest-pose, or overlap-based retrieval at a fixed anchor budget. Table 2 simultaneously changes global versus local representation and single versus multiple anchors, so its large gain cannot be attributed solely to avoiding global fusion.

The principal 500-video evaluation uses 21 context frames interleaved with 49 target frames from the same sampled sequence. This provides useful evidence for history-conditioned view synthesis but does not directly measure causal generation with progressively accumulated synthetic memories. The supplementary stress test partly addresses this gap, but compares only against SPMem and measures returns to the initial viewpoint; it does not establish consistent preservation of newly explored regions across diverse long trajectories.

The strongest claims about global-memory methods depend heavily on the authors' SPMem reimplementation and its accumulated point-cloud representation. Shared training data and backbone are helpful controls, but fidelity to the original method is not validated, and the manuscript does not establish whether practical filtering, consolidation, or bounded-memory variants would show similarly severe quality and scaling failures. The evidence supports the proposed implementation more strongly than a general disadvantage of global geometric memory.

Several details needed for reproduction remain unclear: explicit training/evaluation split separation, alignment of incremental geometry and target camera poses into a common coordinate system, coverage/occlusion computation and FoV thresholds, and pose-weight parameterization. The main text specifies control during 90% of denoising steps whereas the appendix specifies 80%. Small advantages over SEVA also lack uncertainty estimates, and the claim of outperforming all baselines should be qualified because SEVA retains the highest PSNR.
